question: In major US cities from 1900 to 1936, how much of the fall in deaths did researchers credit to filtered, chlorinated water?
answer: Nearly half of the total fall, with about three-quarters of the drop in infant deaths and nearly two-thirds of the drop in child deaths. Typhoid and diarrhoea had been everyday killers. Few people know who chlorinated their city's water; the treatment plant just sits by the river, saving lives nobody counts.
move: The biggest savers of lives are often the dullest-looking machines.
ask: Which unglamorous routine in my life protects me more than anything I would think to boast about?
trap: About a tenth, since doctors and medicines did most of the work.
reference: Cutler & Miller, The role of public health improvements in health advances: the twentieth-century United States, Demography, 2005
